paper.title: Verification of BOUT++ by the Method of Manufactured Solutions

open_questions.q: Does an actual BOUT++ build reproduce the paper's Table 1 error constants (not just the 2nd-order rate) at rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-15, t=10 for the ∇²f Dirichlet MMS problem?
open_questions.basis: The from-scratch replication (REPORT.md §3.5) reproduces the asymptotic 2nd-order slope of the Laplacian operator (1.616→1.816→1.916→1.960→1.981→1.990 across N=8→512) but does NOT match the paper's absolute error magnitudes because the raw operator was tested on a different smooth profile rather than the full 3D time-integrated BOUT++ simulation. This leaves open whether the paper's *specific* Table 1 numbers (e.g. the 1.894 rate dip at N=512, which the report attributes to time-integration tolerance floor) reproduce bit-for-bit today with the shipped examples/MMS runtest script.
open_questions.next_steps: Build BOUT++ with SUNDIALS/PETSc/FFTW/MPI (blocked here by toolchain per §5 item 1); run examples/MMS/diffusion/runtest at N=8,16,32,64,128,256,512 with the paper's tolerances; regenerate Table 1 with the current BOUT++ HEAD and compare rates + absolute ℓ₂/ℓ∞ values against the 2016 paper. A regression here would identify solver/BC drift over ~10 years of BOUT++ evolution.

open_questions.q: Does BOUT++'s WENO limiter converge correctly on non-smooth (shock-like or steep-gradient) manufactured solutions, or is it only verified in the smooth regime where the limiter is inactive?
open_questions.basis: The paper explicitly flags (and the replication §5 item 3 confirms) that smooth-MMS convergence tests do NOT exercise the WENO nonlinear weights / limiter — precisely the mechanism WENO exists for. The smooth-solution test correctly recovers a 2nd-order rate (capped by 2nd-order φ-velocity and BCs), which says nothing about limiter correctness in the shock-capturing regime.
open_questions.next_steps: Design a non-smooth manufactured solution — e.g. a compactly-supported bump with a discontinuous derivative at a known location, or a smoothed-Heaviside profile with tunable steepness parameter ε; measure convergence as ε→0. Alternatively use a MMS with a known-analytic near-shock structure (Burgers-type) as done in shock-capturing literature (Kemm et al., Zhang & Shu). Report whether observed order in the steep-gradient limit remains near 3 (WENO's design order in smooth regions) or degrades gracefully at discontinuities.

open_questions.q: Is the observed 2nd-order cap on the Poisson bracket [φ,f] (which limits both central and WENO advection to 2nd order in the replication) removable by using a higher-order stencil for the φ-derivative — and does BOUT++ have any code path that does so?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md §3.2 reproduces the paper's finding that all four bracket schemes (Arakawa, upwind, central, WENO) are capped at 2nd order because the advection velocity is computed from φ via 2nd-order central differences. This is described as an inherent property, but the report and paper do not resolve whether a higher-order φ-gradient reconstruction (e.g. 4th-order central, or matching the WENO order) would recover the formal 3rd order for WENO.
open_questions.next_steps: Extend code/test_advection.py to include a 4th-order-central and a WENO-reconstructed φ-gradient; re-run the 16²→1024² sweep and compare observed rate against the 2nd-order-φ baseline. Independently, `grep`-audit BOUT++ source for higher-order gradient options on the streamfunction and whether they are default or opt-in; a follow-up MMS on BOUT++ itself with those options enabled would answer whether the code has an unused pathway to 3rd-order advection.

open_questions.q: How do adaptive-order/adaptive-step implicit integrators (SUNDIALS CVODE, PETSc TS) actually behave under MMS forcing, given that both the paper and this replication treat them as untestable black boxes?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md §5 item 2 states that adaptive implicit integrators are inherently unverifiable by fixed-order MMS because the adaptive order/step defeats the fixed-order convergence measurement. This is treated as an acknowledged gap rather than a resolved question — meaning bugs in the adaptive controller (order-selection heuristic, error estimator, step-size safety factor) could be silently masked.
open_questions.next_steps: Two attack angles: (a) run MMS with the adaptive integrator FROZEN at fixed order and fixed step, then walk to the fully-adaptive setting comparing final error norms; the fixed-mode should show clean p-th order convergence, and adaptive mode should not be WORSE than fixed at any tolerance. (b) Vary rtol logarithmically (1e-3…1e-11) with a fixed manufactured solution and check that error(rtol) tracks rtol linearly (the manufactured-solution equivalent of a MMS calibration for adaptive tolerance).

open_questions.q: Does the 2016 BOUT++ verification remain valid for the current BOUT++ HEAD (~a decade of code evolution: shifted-metric refactor, GPU kernels, new solver bindings) — i.e. is a 2026 re-run of examples/MMS/*/runtest still passing?
open_questions.basis: REPORT.md provenance and §5 note that the paper's own reproduction path (examples/MMS/*/runtest) ships with BOUT++ and is claimed reproducible in principle, but no re-run against the current HEAD is reported anywhere in the replication artifact. A verification result is only as durable as the code it was measured against; refactors and new backends can silently break MMS convergence without breaking regression tests.
open_questions.next_steps: Clone BOUT++ HEAD; check whether examples/MMS/{time_integration, advection, wave, diffusion} still exist under those names (10 years of refactor risk); run each runtest and produce a side-by-side of 2016 paper rates vs 2026 rates. Optionally bisect any regression to the offending commit. This is the natural follow-up whenever BOUT++ toolchain access is available (the current replication was toolchain-blocked).
